paras: The lynching of George Jones was the killing of a Black prisoner by a masked mob that broke into the county jail at Mayersville, Mississippi, on the night of September 1, 1903. Jones had been arrested on a charge of arson, and the mob shot him so many times that his body was described as "literally riddled with bullets." The killing drew only brief notice, though an Atlanta editorial against lynching soon cited a Mississippi lynching over arson as proof that mobs no longer acted only to punish rape.

Jones, described in the reports as "a negro," was held in the county jail at Mayersville after his arrest on a charge of arson. Neither report says what he was accused of burning or when he was arrested.

On the night of September 1, a mob broke into the jail where Jones was held. According to a dispatch telegraphed from Mayersville the next day, all of the members of the mob were masked. They shot Jones in the jail; his body was "literally riddled with bullets." The reports give no size for the mob, name none of its members, and do not mention a jailer or any resistance.
No report of an inquest, arrests, or grand jury action appears in the coverage.

The New-York Tribune carried the earliest and fullest account on September 3, a telegraphed dispatch headed "Lynched on a Charge of Arson" with the subhead "Mob, All Masked, Break Into Mississippi Jail—Negro Riddled with Bullets." Nine days later the Brookhaven Leader, a Mississippi paper, reduced the story to a single sentence under the headline "Mob Kills a Negro." Both papers stated the arson charge and the killing without comment.

On September 14 the Atlanta Constitution, in an editorial praising Bishop Warren A. Candler's attack on lynching, noted that "a Mississippi lynching was inspired by an attempt at arson." Naming neither place nor victim, it used the example, with cases from Indiana and Illinois, to argue that lynching was no longer reserved for the crime of rape. No Black-press account of the killing appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Lynching of George Jones
bases: A masked mob broke into a county jail and shot to death a Black prisoner held on an arson charge (A1, A2).

The Tribune says the mob 'lynched' Jones and riddled his body with bullets, and the Leader heads its brief 'Mob Kills a Negro' (A1, A2); a masked mob of several members took him from jail, where he was held on a charge of arson (A1, A2).

The Tribune's telegraphed dispatch (A1) is the only full report; the Leader's undated one-sentence brief (A2) agrees on every point but adds nothing and is probably a condensation of the same dispatch, and the Atlanta editorial (A3) names neither place nor victim.
